touches.text: Tool: a complete primitive. Has users, not an owner. Calls no other Cairn component (stdlib and base only) and owns no state of its own. Lives in cairn/tools/ (17). Its data for a holder lives under that holder: ~/.cairn/devices/<device>/<instance>/tools/<tool>/.

Machine: tools plus the glue that holds them together. Has an owner. Anything that calls another component, uses other tools, or owns state it must gate is a machine. Lives inside its device (cairn/devices/<device>/machines/<machine>/), or in cairn/machines/ when several devices hold one (16).
A device talks to other devices only over the bus, never by importing them.
The exceptions are client tools a device publishes:
Librarian: the embedding links work better without device boundaries in the way (4.5.2).
Trouble: it has to be able to report when nothing else can, so a direct line makes sense for recovery (6.3.4).

Scratch bus: a proof needs a bus it controls (a real store, stub devices, nobody live listening), so the cairn device publishes scratch_bus, the way db_domain's client carries scratch(). Akien 2026-11-12, answering Q#86 (8 proof imports of the bus machine in tester, codemother and librarian, measured 2026-11-11): "works for me". 2.3.8Every device has the panes the base shim defines (17.1.3.5.2), drawn by the web server (15):

Ownership. The librarian owns every tree and delegates some to the devices that learn. EVERYTHING THAT LEARNS USING OUR GRAPH TREES IS A DELEGATE (CodeMother, chart and any learning block are examples, not a list), and each holds its trees by the librarian's delegation (Law 6: delegation through the owner's gate). WHY: two holders with different weights over the same nodes have different perspectives and can debate points, and the librarian, asked anything, can look at the query from both.
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).

It is the READY TO MERGE ONTO MAIN step of the pipeline: everything's proved, and merging implies pushing it up. With a branch per ticket (3.3.6), commits on the branch are as often as we like; the inspector is the step at ready to merge. Checking what a change touched belongs here; nothing hangs off the git post-commit hook.
PURPOSE: Wrap a service so there is exactly one way to it.
WHY: One way means one place to authenticate, meter, route and gate, and one place RULE 1 can be enforced by physics (import_sieve, 17.13).
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.

The RULE 1 check is a path check: code inside device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo (anything not under cairn.devices.bar), except a tool foo publishes (cairn.devices.foo.tools.<x>, its charter saying published_by_device). Inside one device there is one owner, so nothing is checked there. A charter's public_interface describes what the component offers (modules, functions, bus verbs, commands); the check does not read it. Akien 2026-11-09 (Q#77): "wouldn't it be easier (for the python code anyway) to see if the imports do not include other device paths?"

conflicts.ticket_says: one sieve in build_inspector reds every cross-component import that does not land in the target's declared interface (where each charter declares `public_interface` — the dotted modules others may import)
conflicts.why: The outline explicitly states at 17.13.1: 'A charter's public_interface describes what the component offers (modules, functions, bus verbs, commands); the check does not read it.' The check is described as path-based only. The ticket proposes making the check machine-readable against the declared interface specification, which contradicts the outline's statement that the check does not read public_interface. Akien's Q#77 comment reinforces the path-check approach, not interface-declaration checking.
